chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ali ibn al-Hakam, from Bashir ibn Hamza, from a man from Quraish who said:

A cousin of mine sent a message to me; she had much wealth. You know the abundance of men proposing to me, but I did not marry them myself. I did not send for you out of desire for men, but rather because it reached me that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, permitted it in His Book, and the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) explained it in his Sunnah, but Zafar prohibited it. So I desired to obey Allah, Mighty and Majestic, above His Throne, and to obey the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family), and to disobey Zafar. So marry me by way of Mut'ah.
So I said to her, 'Not until I go to Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) and consult him.'
So I went to him and informed him. He said, 'Do it. May Allah send blessings upon both of you as spouses.'
ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on temporary marriage (Mut'ah) according to Shia hadith?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi highlights the juristic debate surrounding temporary marriage (Mut'ah) by contrasting the Quranic and Prophetic basis with the specific prohibition attributed to Zafar (often identified as Zafar al-Hadrami or a companion). The narrator’s decision to consult Imam al-Sadiq (AS) and receive his approval underscores the Shia reliance on the Imams for clarifying legal nuances and validating practices that may have been contested by other schools of thought. It serves as a key textual evidence for the enduring validity of Mut'ah in Shia jurisprudence despite historical disagreements.
